§ 3PRIME MINISTER AND COUNCIL OF MINISTERS

(Article 74-78)

  • The Prime Minister (PM) is considered as the Head of the Council who assists the President of India is the Chairman of the:
  • The Prime Minister of India is the Chairman of the:
  • NITI AAYOG
  • Interstate Council
  • National Disaster Management Authority
  • The PM is known as the Real / De facto head of the government. (President is known as De jure / Nominal head.)

Article 74: Council of Ministers to aid and advise President

74(1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister as the head to aid and advise the President who shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers.

- 42nd Constitutional Amendment made the advise binding on President.
- 44th Constitutional Amendment: President may request the Council of Ministers to reconsider advice however after reconsideration, the President must ultimately act according to the advice tendered.

74(2) The question, whether any, and if so what advice was tendered by ministers to the President shall not be inquired into by any court.

- 44th CA, 1978 introduced the term "Cabinet" for the first time formally (into the Constitution.)
- Specifically, in Article 352(3), which states that Emergency must be based on a written recommendation of the "Cabinet."

Article 75: Other provisions as to Ministers

75(1) The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and other ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.

91st Amendment, 2003 added -
- (1A) The total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
- (1B) If any member is disqualified on the grounds of defection, they cannot become minister.

75(2) Ministers hold office till the pleasure of the President.

75(3) Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

75(4) Before entering office, the Prime Minister and Ministers must take oaths of office and secrecy administered by the President.

75(5) A Minister who is not a member of either Houses of the Parliament for six consecutive months shall cease to be a Minister at the end of that period.

75(6) Salaries and allowances of Ministers are determined by Parliament and until Parliament fixes that, it shall be as specified in the 2nd Schedule.

Types of Ministers (not specified by the Constitution):

  • Cabinet Ministers: Important portfolios like Defence, Home, Finance, Education, Health. Participate in Cabinet meetings.
  • Minister of State: Handle smaller ministries or assist Cabinet Ministers. Do not participate in Cabinet meetings.
  • Deputy Ministers: Assist Cabinet Ministers and Ministers of State.

Hierarchy diagram: PM → Cabinet → Minister of State → Deputy Minister

Article 76: Attorney General of India

76(1) President shall appoint a person who is qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court to be Attorney General of India.

76(2) Duty: To give advice to the Government of India upon legal matters.

76(3) Attorney General has the right to audience in all courts within the territory of India.

76(4) Attorney General holds office till the pleasure of the President and receives remuneration as determined by the President.

POINTS TO REMEMBER:

  • He is not a full-time counsel of the government.
  • He is not debarred from the private legal practice, after ceasing to hold office.
  • 1st Attorney General: M. C. Setalvad (longest serving)
  • Current Attorney General: R. Venkataramani
  • He is the highest law officer of the country.

Solicitor General of India:

  • Assists Attorney General but is not a constitutional post.
  • Current Solicitor General of India: Tushar Mehta

Advocate General of State (Article 165)

  • Appointed by Governor.
  • Must be qualified to be a judge of a High Court.
  • Duty: Advise State Government on legal matters.
  • Holds office during the pleasure of the Governor.
  • He is the highest law officer of the state.

Dissolution of Council of Ministers (CoM)

  • If any member of Council of Ministers Resigns / Dies / Removed then vacancy is created.
  • If the Prime Minister dies or resigns then entire CoMs is dissolved, in that case entire CoMs has to resign, the President invites the leader with majority's support in the LS to become the new PM.
First Indian PM to resign - Morarji Desai

Rajya Sabha Members who became PM:

  • Indira Gandhi
  • Manmohan Singh
  • H. D. Deve Gowda (He became the PM of India without becoming a Union Cabinet Minister)

Article 77: Conduct of Business of the Government of India

77(1) All executive actions of Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President.

77(2) Orders and instruments made in the name of the President shall be authenticated in such manner as specified in rules made by the President.

77(3) The President shall make rules for more convenient transaction of the business of Government of India and allocate responsibilities among Ministers.

Article 78: Duties of Prime Minister

(a) To communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration of the Union and proposals for legislation.

(b) To furnish such information relating to the administration of the Union and proposals for legislation as the President may call for.

(c) If the President so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council.

Comments on the post of PM

  • "Collective responsibility can be achieved only through the instrumentality of the Prime Minister." — Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.
  • Pt. J.L. Nehru described PM as "The Linchpin of Government"; as the PM acts as a link between the Council of Ministers and the President.

Diagram: Council of Ministers — PM — President (Acts as linkage - Article 78)

Summarising the Powers and Functions of the PM:

  • Advises President regarding summoning and proroguing of the sessions of the Parliament.
  • Recommends dissolution of Lok Sabha to President any time.
  • Announces government policies on the floor of the House.
  • Recommends names for ministerial appointments.
  • Allocates and reshuffles portfolios among ministers.
  • Can ask a Minister to resign or recommend dismissal.
  • Presides over Council of Ministers meetings.
  • Guides, directs, controls and coordinates activities of Ministers.
  • Can cause collapse of the Council of Ministers by resigning.

Few PMs of India and their term of office:

  • Jawaharlal Nehru: Longest serving Prime Minister (16 years, 286 days).
  • Atal Bihari Vajpayee: Served an initial 13-day term as Prime Minister.
  • Chaudhary Charan Singh: 170 days.
  • Chandra Shekhar: 7 months. (Shortest serving amongst all full term PMs)
  • V. P. Singh: 11 months.
  • H. D. Deve Gowda: 10 months.
  • Inder Kumar Gujral: 11 months.

P. Singh 1989-1990, Narasimha Rao 1991-1996, Deve Gowda 1996-1997, I. K. Gujral 1997-1998, Vajpayee 1998-2004, Manmohan Singh 2004-2014, Narendra Modi 2014-Present)

§ 4EMERGENCY

  • Emergency Provisions are mentioned under Part XVIII of the Constitution in Article: 352-360
  • They are borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany.
  • There are three types of Emergency:
  1. 1. National Emergency (President's rule)
  2. 2. State Emergency
  3. 3. Financial Emergency

Article 352: National Emergency

Proclamation:

  • Proclamation of Emergency is made by the President after receiving a decision from Cabinet. (44th amendment)
  • Proclamation must be approved within 1 month from the date of its issue by both the Houses of the Parliament with a Special Majority.
  • If approved it continues for 6 Months & can be extended to an indefinite time period after the approval of Parliament after every 6 Months.
  • Minerva Mills Case vs Union of India, 1980:
  • Proclamation of emergency is subject to Judicial Review.

Grounds of Proclamation:

  • War
  • External Aggression
  • Armed Rebellion: This term was inserted by the 44th Amendment, 1978. Before that it was known as Internal Disturbance.

Revocation:

  • Emergency can be revoked any time by the President without any requirement for Parliamentary approval.
  • But, if Lok Sabha passes a resolution just by Simple Majority approving the discontinuation of Emergency then in that case President must revoke the Emergency.
The term "Cabinet" was inserted in Art 352 of Constitution in 1978 by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act.

Effects of National Emergency

#### 1) Effects on Centre State Relations

  • Federal system becomes Unitary in nature
  • During Non-emergency times centre can give directions to state on some specified matters but during Emergency it can give directions on any matter.
  • During Emergency Parliament is empowered to make laws on any subject mentioned in the state list. (These laws become inoperative 6 months after Emergency ceases to operate.)

#### 2) Effects on the Life of Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly

  • It may be extended for 1 year at a time, but this extension cannot continue beyond a period of 6 months after the emergency has ceased to operate.

#### 3) Effect on Fundamental Rights

Article 358Article 359
It deals with suspension of FRs guaranteed by Article 19.It deals with suspension of other FRs.
Article 19 can only be suspended on the grounds of war and external aggression and not in case of armed rebellion.It empowers the President to suspend "Right to move any court" for enforcement of FRs except Article 20 and 21. (Can never be suspended.)

National Emergencies Declaration Till Now

  • 1962: Indo-China War (Oct 1962-1968) (Then PM: J L Nehru)
  • 1971: India and Pakistan War (Then PM: Indira Gandhi)
  • 1975: Internal Disturbances (1975-1977) (Then PM: Indira Gandhi) (President: Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed)
25th June: Samvidhan Hatya Diwas

Article 355: Duty of Centre to protect every state against external aggression.

Article 355 act as the foundation for the centre to intervene in a state under Article 356 when necessary, creating a clear correlation between two provisions.

Article 356: President's Rule (State Emergency / Constitutional Emergency)

Grounds:

  • If a situation has arisen in which the government of the state cannot be carried on, in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.
  • Whenever a state fails to comply with or to give effect to any direction from the centre.

Approval:

  • Must be approved by both the Houses of Parliament with a simple majority within 2 months from the date of its issue.
  • If approved it continues for 6 months and can be extended for a maximum period of 3 Years.

Proclamation:

  • By the President of India which can be done only after cabinet approval. (44th CAA, 1978)

Revocation:

  • Any time by the President, no need of Parliamentary approval or
  • If LS passes a resolution through Simple Majority.

Consequences:

  • President can take up the functions of Governor
  • Parliament can take up the functions of State Legislature
  • Executive is dismissed and Legislature is either suspended or dissolved.

Use of Article 356

  • For the 1st time President Rule was imposed in Punjab in 1951.
  • Manipur has undergone the President's Rule the most number of times(11).
  • In Uttar Pradesh, President Rule was imposed 10 times.
B. R. Ambedkar about Article 356: "It should be used as a last resort and as a means of final recourse."
There is no effect on FRs during president's rule.
S. R. Bommai Case (1994): Significantly curtailed the misuse of Article 356 and held that President's rule is subject to Judicial Review.

Article 360: Financial Emergency

Proclamation:

  • Article 360 empowers President to proclaim a Financial Emergency if he is satisfied that financial stability of India or any of its part has been threatened.
  • It is approved by the Parliament within 2 months by a Simple Majority (same as President's Rule)
  • No Financial Emergency has been imposed till now.
  • During the Financial Emergency, the President can ask the States to reduce the salaries and allowances of all or any class of person in government services.

Committees that deal with Centre-State Relations

  • Sarkaria Commission: 1983
  • Punchhi Commission: 2007
  • Rajmannar Commission: 1969 (setup by Tamil Nadu government)

Inter-State Council (ISC)

  • Article 263 of the Indian Constitution establishes the Inter-State Council (ISC) to address inter-State issues and foster harmonious relations between the States and the Union.

Composition of the Inter-State Council:

  • Chairman: Prime Minister
  • Members:
  • Chief Ministers of all States
  • Chief Ministers of Union Territories with Legislative Assemblies
  • Administrators of Union Territories without Legislative Assemblies
  • Six Cabinet Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister of India.

Zonal Councils

  • Zonal Councils are the statutory (and not the constitutional) bodies. They are established by an Act of the Parliament, States Reorganisation Act of 1956.
  • The act divided the country into five zones- Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern and provided a zonal council for each zone.

Composition of the Zonal Council:

  • Chairman: Union Home Minister
  • Vice Chairman: Chief Ministers of the States included in each zone act as Vice-Chairman for that zone by rotation, each holding office for a period of one year at a time.
The North Eastern Council was constituted in 1971 by an Act of Parliament.

§ 5PART XX - CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT

Basic Pointers:

  • Borrowed from the Constitution of South Africa.
  • Article 368: Deals with the procedure of Amendment.
  • Parliament cannot amend those provision which form the Basic structure of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharti Case, 1973)
Basic Structure of Constitution is not Mentioned in the Constitution but was Born in Kesavananda Bharti Case (1973) & has evolved in further cases.
It Consists of:
Judicial Review, Independent Judiciary, Separation of Powers, Federal Structure, Secularism, Supremacy of Constitution.

Procedure:

  • Constitutional Amendment Bill can be introduced in either house of Parliament (LS/RS) but not in State Legislature
  • Can be introduced by any minister or a private member.
  • It does not require the prior recommendation of President for introduction.
  • President must give his/her assent & no veto is allowed in case of a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368. (24th CA, 1971)
  • There is no provision of joint sitting in the case of a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

Types of Amendments

1. By simple majority of Parliament:

  • It is outside the purview of Article 368.
  • It is amended in the same way as normal legislations are passed.

2. By special majority of Parliament:

  • For amending provisions, not within the first category.
  • This requires both a Majority of total membership of each House and, a Majority of not less than 2/3rd of the members present and voting of each House. (As per article 368)

3. Special Majority + Ratification of atleast 1/2 of the State Legislatures:

  • It is related to the federal structure of polity.
  • Amendment - Special Majority of Parliament + State Ratification by Simple Majority.

Provisions Amended by Simple Majority:

  • Admission/establishment of new state
  • Formation of new states, alteration of boundaries, areas, names of states.
  • 2nd Schedule
  • 5th/6th Schedule
  • Quorum in Parliament
  • Delimitation of Constituencies
  • To create/abolish Legislative Council
  • Use of official language
  • Election to Parliament and state legislatures
  • Union territories
  • Salaries and allowances of members of Parliament.

Provisions Amended by Special Majority:

  • Fundamental Rights
  • DPSP
  • Fundamental Duties

Provisions Amended by Special Majority + Ratification of at least 1/2 of the States:

  • Election of President and its manner
  • Supreme Court/High Court
  • Article 368, itself.
  • Any list in 7th Schedule
  • Distribution of Legislative powers between centre and states.
  • Representation of states in Parliament.

Comments on Amending Procedure:

  1. 1. This variety of amending process is wise, but rarely found: K. C. Wheare
  2. 2. Strikes a good balance between rigidity and flexibility: K.C. Wheare
  3. 3. The amending process has proved itself one of the most ably conceived aspects of the Constitution, Although it appears complicated, it is merely diverse: Granville Austin

Recent Constitutional Amendments (CA):

  • 100 CA, 2015: India-Bangladesh land boundary agreement
  • 101 CA, 2016: GST
  • 102 CA, 2018: National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) (Gave Constitutional status)
  • 103 CA, 2019: Economically Weaker Section (EWS) (10% reservation given)
  • 104 CA, 2020: Removal of Anglo Indians nomination from Lok Sabha and state assemblies
  • 105 CA, 2021: It restored the power of state government to identify the Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs)
  • 106 CA, 2023: 1/3rd seats in LS/LA reserved for women
  • (Important Amendments have been separately dealt in each chapter.)
Do you know?
42nd Amendment is also known as Mini Constitution due to extensive changes it brought to our constitution.

§ 6Key concepts

  • Prime Minister as head of Council of Ministers (Article 74-78)
  • Collective responsibility to Lok Sabha (Article 75(3))

  • Pardoning Power and 42nd & 44th Constitutional Amendments on binding advice
  • PM's powers - summoning Parliament, dissolution of Lok Sabha, Council meetings
  • National Emergency (Article 352)
  • President's Rule (Article 356)
  • Financial Emergency (Article 360)
  • Constitutional Amendment (Article 368)
  • Basic Structure Doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati 1973)
